claims.text: What the image looks like Ring-enhancing lesion(s) (with contrast)
claims.quote: Ring-enhancing lesion(s) (with contrast)

claims.text: Brain abscess: a fully developed abscess appears as an edematous mass with ring enhancement, which may be difficult to distinguish from a brain tumor or occasionally infarction; CT-guided aspiration, culture, surgical excision or a combination may be necessary
claims.quote: A fully developed abscess appears as an edematous mass with ring enhancement, which may be difficult to distinguish from a brain tumor or occasionally infarction; CT-guided aspiration, culture, surgical excision, or a combination may be necessary.

claims.text: Example gadolinium-enhanced MRI: a cerebellar abscess appearing as a large, rim-enhancing cavitary lesion in the left cerebellar hemisphere
claims.quote: This gadolinium-enhanced MRI scan shows a cerebellar abscess, which appears as a large, rim-enhancing cavitary lesion in the left cerebellar hemisphere.

claims.text: Suspected CNS toxoplasmosis: head CT and/or MRI with contrast (MRI is more sensitive), plus LP if there are no signs of increased ICP; imaging typically shows single or multiple, rounded, ring-enhancing lesions
claims.quote: If central nervous system (CNS) toxoplasmosis is suspected, patients should have head CT with contrast, MRI with contrast, or both plus a lumbar puncture if there are no signs of increased intracranial pressure. MRI is more sensitive than CT. MRI and CT with contrast typically show single or multiple, rounded, ring-enhancing lesions.

claims.text: Buzzword: ring-enhancing lesions on CT/MRI brain → abscess, toxoplasmosis (HIV), GBM, mets
claims.quote: Ring-enhancing lesions CT/MRI brain Abscess, toxoplasmosis (HIV), GBM, mets

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) Symmetry: gray-white differentiation, ventricles, sulci, basal cisterns
claims.quote: Symmetry - gray-white differentiation, ventricles, sulci, basal cisterns.

claims.text: Brain: gray-white preservation; look for sulcal effacement, mass effect, midline shift
claims.quote: Brain - gray-white preservation, sulcal effacement, mass effect, midline shift.

claims.text: Cisterns: basal/suprasellar (5-pointed star); effaced = herniation risk
claims.quote: Cisterns - basal/suprasellar (5-pointed star); effaced = herniation risk.

claims.text: Ventricles: symmetric size; trapped temporal horn = early hydrocephalus
claims.quote: Ventricles - symmetric size; trapped temporal horn = early hydrocephalus.

claims.text: Suspected abscess: contrast-enhanced MRI with diffusion-weighted images or, if MRI is unavailable, contrast-enhanced CT
claims.quote: When symptoms suggest an abscess, contrast-enhanced MRI with diffusion-weighted images or, if MRI is unavailable, contrast-enhanced CT is done.

claims.text: Causes Her chart: brain abscess; toxoplasmosis (HIV); GBM; metastasis
claims.quote: Brain abscess; toxoplasmosis (HIV); GBM; metastasis

claims.text: A brain abscess can result from: direct extension of cranial infections (eg, osteomyelitis, mastoiditis, sinusitis, subdural empyema); penetrating head wounds (including neurosurgery); hematogenous spread (eg, endocarditis, congenital heart disease with right-to-left shunt, IV drug use); unknown causes
claims.quote: A brain abscess can result from (1): Direct extension of cranial infections (eg, osteomyelitis, mastoiditis, sinusitis, subdural empyema) Penetrating head wounds (including neurosurgical procedures) Hematogenous spread (eg, in bacterial endocarditis [2], congenital heart disease with right-to-left shunt, or IV drug use) Unknown causes

claims.text: Abscess bacteria are usually anaerobic and sometimes mixed; staphylococci are commonly involved after cranial trauma, neurosurgery or endocarditis
claims.quote: The bacteria involved are usually anaerobic and sometimes mixed, often including anaerobes such as Bacteroides and anaerobic and microaerophilic streptococci. Staphylococci are commonly involved after cranial trauma, neurosurgery, or endocarditis.

claims.text: Fungi (eg, Aspergillus) and protozoa (eg, Toxoplasma gondii, particularly with HIV) can cause abscesses
claims.quote: Fungi (eg, Aspergillus) and protozoa (eg, Toxoplasma gondii, particularly in patients with HIV infection) can cause abscesses.

claims.text: Most immunocompromised patients who develop toxoplasmosis present with encephalitis and ring-enhancing intracranial mass lesions on contrast CT or MRI
claims.quote: Most immunocompromised patients who develop toxoplasmosis present with encephalitis and ring-enhancing intracranial mass lesions seen on CT or MRI scans both with contrast.

claims.text: Tissue cysts can reactivate, primarily in immunocompromised patients: toxoplasmosis reactivates in advanced HIV without antibiotic prophylaxis; widespread trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole for Pneumocystis prophylaxis has dramatically reduced the incidence
claims.quote: The cysts can reactivate, causing disease, primarily in immunocompromised patients. Toxoplasmosis reactivates in patients with advanced HIV infection who are not taking antibiotic prophylaxis, but the widespread use of trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole for Pneumocystis prophylaxis has dramatically reduced the incidence (1).

claims.text: Symptoms Brain abscess: headache, nausea, vomiting, lethargy, seizures, personality changes, papilledema and focal neurologic deficits develop over days to weeks; fever may be absent at presentation
claims.quote: Headache, nausea, vomiting, lethargy, seizures, personality changes, papilledema, and focal neurologic deficits develop over days to weeks; fever may be absent at presentation.

claims.text: Toxoplasmosis: risk is greatest with HIV and a CD4 count < 50/mcL (toxoplasmic encephalitis is rare when CD4 > 200/mcL); these patients typically have headache, altered mental status, seizures, coma, fever, and sometimes focal deficits (motor or sensory loss, cranial nerve palsies, visual abnormalities, focal seizures)
claims.quote: Risk is greatest among patients with HIV infection who have a CD4 count < 50/mcL; toxoplasmic encephalitis is rare when CD4 counts are > 200/mcL. These patients typically have headache, altered mental status, seizures, coma, fever, and sometimes focal neurologic deficits, such as motor or sensory loss, cranial nerve palsies, visual abnormalities, and focal seizures.

claims.text: Treatment and next step Her chart: MRI characterizes; biopsy or empiric therapy by context
claims.quote: MRI characterizes; biopsy or empiric therapy by context

claims.text: Brain abscess: treat all with antibiotics (usually initially ceftriaxone or cefotaxime, plus metronidazole if Bacteroides is suspected or plus vancomycin if S. aureus is suspected), typically followed by CT-guided stereotactic aspiration or surgical drainage
claims.quote: Treat all brain abscesses with antibiotics (usually initially with ceftriaxone or cefotaxime plus metronidazole if clinicians suspect Bacteroides species or plus vancomycin if they suspect S. aureus), typically followed by CT-guided stereotactic aspiration or surgical drainage.

claims.text: Drainage is necessary for most solitary, surgically accessible abscesses, particularly those > 2 cm; if < 2 cm, antibiotics alone may be tried with frequent serial MRI or CT (initially as often as every 2 to 3 days), and enlargement on antibiotics indicates surgical drainage
claims.quote: Drainage (CT-guided stereotactic or open) provides optimal therapy and is necessary for most abscesses that are solitary and surgically accessible, particularly those > 2 cm in diameter. If abscesses are < 2 cm in diameter, antibiotics alone may be tried, but abscesses must then be monitored with frequent serial MRI or CT (initially as often as every 2 to 3 days); if abscesses enlarge after being treated with antibiotics, surgical drainage is indicated.

claims.text: Brain abscess: lumbar puncture is not done, because it may precipitate transtentorial herniation and CSF findings are nonspecific
claims.quote: Lumbar puncture is not done because it may precipitate transtentorial herniation and because cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings are nonspecific

claims.text: Toxoplasmosis: these lesions are not pathognomonic, but in advanced HIV with CNS symptoms they warrant a trial of chemotherapy for T. gondii
claims.quote: Although these lesions are not pathognomonic, their presence in patients with advanced HIV infection and CNS symptoms warrants a trial of chemotherapy for T. gondii.

claims.text: Toxoplasmosis: pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine plus leucovorin (to prevent bone marrow suppression), or trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole in some situations; clindamycin or atovaquone plus pyrimethamine when the patient is allergic to sulfonamides or does not tolerate sulfadiazine
claims.quote: Pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine plus leucovorin (to prevent bone marrow suppression); alternatively, the fixed drug combination trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole in some situations Clindamycin or atovaquone plus pyrimethamine when the patient is allergic to sulfonamides or does not tolerate sulfadiazine

claims.text: After successful treatment, chronic maintenance therapy prevents relapse in patients who remain immunocompromised (relapse is particularly common with advanced HIV and CD4 < 200/mcL); it continues until CD4 stays > 200/mcL for > 6 months on antiretroviral therapy
claims.quote: Chronic maintenance therapy is used after successful treatment of acute disease to prevent relapses in patients who remain immunocompromised. Relapses are particularly common in patients with advanced HIV infection who have a CD4 count < 200/mcL. Maintenance therapy is continued until the CD4 count remains > 200/mcL for > 6 months on antiretroviral therapy.
